analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts through independent commissions and bans mid-decade remapping.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress, despite 9 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states from redrawing congressional district maps more than once after each census, closing the door on mid-decade gerrymandering. It would require every state to hand map-drawing to an independent commission whose meetings are public, which cannot consider voters' party affiliation or where incumbents live, and which must take public input through a state website with interactive mapping tools. If a legislature rejected the commission's plan, the state's highest court — or a federal court — would pick or draw the plan instead, and the federal government would pay states $150,000 per congressional seat to run the process.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters benefit most. Districts would be drawn without regard to party performance or incumbent addresses, which tends to produce maps that follow county, city, and neighborhood lines rather than political calculations [S3]. Voters would be able to watch the process in real time: all commission meetings would be open to the public, and each state would have to run a website with census and voting data, interactive software letting anyone design and submit their own map, and seven days' advance public notice before a plan goes to the legislature [S3]. Because maps could not be redrawn mid-decade, the districts voters choose under in a given decade would be the ones they keep [S2][S3]. Voters whose districts were gerrymandered to guarantee one party's control would have a better chance of elections that actually depend on their votes.

how_it_helps.text: Bans a second congressional redistricting after a census unless a court orders one to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act, ending the practice of legislatures remapping districts mid-decade for political advantage [S2][S3].

Requires each state to establish an independent commission, appointed in equal numbers by the majority and minority parties in both legislative chambers, with members barred from having held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the previous four years, and barred from running for Congress until after the next apportionment [S3].

Prohibits the commission from considering voters' party affiliation, past voting history, or the home addresses of incumbent House members when drawing districts — the three inputs used to build safe seats [S3].

Opens the process to the public: every meeting public, a state website with precinct-level census and voting data, interactive software for citizens to draw and submit their own plans, and seven days' published notice before any plan reaches the legislature, including any dissenting statements from commissioners [S3].

Sets map-drawing criteria that put geography over politics: districts must stay as whole as possible at the county, municipal, and neighborhood levels, be compact and contiguous, with essentially equal population [S3].

If the legislature rejects the commission's plan, the state's highest court must choose among submitted plans without modification, and if that fails, the local U.S. district court draws the map — so a legislature cannot simply block reform by doing nothing [S3].
Funds the process with a federal payment of $150,000 per congressional seat (authorized for all states with more than one Representative), conditioned on actually establishing the commission [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislative majorities that currently draw the maps would lose their control over district boundaries: the bill strips legislatures of the power to amend a commission plan (they could only approve or reject it as written) and outlaws map-drawing that takes incumbents' residences or party performance into account [S3]. Taxpayers generally would fund the commission operations, through authorized federal payments of $150,000 per congressional seat — roughly $65 million nationally for a 435-seat House once per decade, a small sum for a federal program [S3].

drawbacks.text: The commission is not fully independent of the politicians it regulates: members are appointed by the top legislative leaders of the two largest parties in each chamber, so the same party establishment that draws maps today would choose the map-drawers [S3].

The state legislature could still reject the commission's plan, forcing courts to pick or draw the map — a fallback that adds delay and leaves judges, not voters, with the final word in states where the legislature refuses to cooperate [S3].

It is a one-size-fits-all federal mandate on how all 50 states run redistricting, overriding state constitutional arrangements, and it would apply only to maps drawn after the 2020 census — meaning even if passed in 2013, it would have changed nothing for the districts then in use [S3].

The commission terminates after the first federal general election of the cycle, so the public transparency machinery (website, meetings, input process) disappears after one use each decade, and any bad map would be locked in until the next census absent a court order [S3].

States would bear the administrative work of building and operating a commission, with federal payments ($150,000 per seat) conditioned on establishing one — a modest cost, but real, and single-member states get nothing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct costs are small — about $150,000 per congressional seat in federal money to operate a commission once per decade [S3] — while the potential effect is structural: who controls the drawing of every congressional district in the country. The design is not perfect. Commission members would still be appointed by the same party leaders who gerrymander today, legislatures could reject commission plans and push map-drawing into the courts, and the bill would not have touched any map in effect before the 2020 census [S3]. But taken on its own terms, the trade is modest spending and some state-legislature power given up, in exchange for districts drawn without reference to party performance or incumbents' addresses, with the whole process conducted in public. The bill's biggest weakness is that it never got far enough for anyone to test whether the commission design would work in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Barrow introduced the bill on January 14, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On January 25, 2013, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice; that was the last action of any kind [S5].

Nine members — 8 Democrats and 1 Republican — signed on as cosponsors, but the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber during the two-year Congress [S4][S5].
The bill died on January 3, 2015, when the 113th Congress ended and all unfinished legislation expired [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the state legislative majorities that draw congressional maps are better off: they keep the power to redraw districts whenever they want and to draw lines with party performance and incumbents' homes in mind, which the bill would have taken away.

for.name: Rep. John Barrow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made it the vehicle for the independent-commission approach named after former Rep. John Tanner.

for.name: House cosponsors (8 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support, giving the bill sponsorship from both parties.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 14, 2013, sent it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, and never held a markup or a vote on it [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from January 25, 2013 onward and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; no vote was ever scheduled in either chamber of Congress [S5].

against.name: Incumbent members of both parties who benefit from legislatively drawn districts
against.role: Members of Congress whose seats are protected by gerrymandered maps
against.what_they_did: The bill would have stripped map-drawing power from legislatures and barred consideration of incumbents' residences; few members of either party had an incentive to advance it, and only 1 of 435 members beyond the sponsor's cosponsors list from the Republican conference ever signed on.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded, so the partisan split was never measured; the 9 cosponsors were 8 Democrats and 1 Republican, and the committee that buried the bill was controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: State legislative majorities that draw congressional maps
industries.note: The bill removes their core power: drawing the congressional districts that determine which party holds House seats. It reduces legislatures to an up-or-down vote on a commission plan they cannot amend, and hands map-drawing to courts if they refuse [S3]. Their interest in keeping that power runs directly against voters' interest in non-partisan maps.

The bill forbids map-drawers from considering where incumbents live or how districts have voted in the past, the inputs used to build safe seats [S3]. Combined with the mid-decade remapping ban, incumbents would face districts they could not tailor to themselves and could not redraw when their positions weakened.

Commission members could not have worked for a party or candidate in the prior four years, and the commission could not use voters' party affiliation — eliminating the data-driven partisan mapmaking that both national parties have invested in [S3].
